title: Plant Kingdom
description: Grade 11 Biology: algae (green, brown, red), bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms, plus plant life cycles and alternation of generations. Notes and a test.

topics.title: Algae
topics.concept:
Kingdom Plantae includes all eukaryotic, multicellular, chlorophyll-containing organisms that make their own food (photosynthetic autotrophs). The plant kingdom is divided into algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms.

Algae are simple, chlorophyll-bearing, mostly aquatic plants (also found in moist soil, on stones and on other plants). Their body is a simple thallus (not differentiated into root, stem and leaf). They reproduce by vegetative, asexual (spores) and sexual methods. Based on their pigments, stored food and cell-wall composition, algae are grouped into three classes:

  • Chlorophyceae (green algae) — green because of chlorophyll a and b; store food as starch; cell wall of cellulose. Examples: Chlamydomonas, Spirogyra, Ulothrix, Volvox.
  • Phaeophyceae (brown algae) — brown due to the pigment fucoxanthin (plus chlorophyll a and c); store food as laminarin/mannitol; mostly marine. Examples: Laminaria, Fucus, Sargassum, Ectocarpus.
  • Rhodophyceae (red algae) — red due to the pigment r-phycoerythrin; store food as floridean starch; mostly marine, found even in deep water. Examples: Polysiphonia, Gracilaria, Gelidium.

Algae are economically important: they perform about half of the total photosynthesis (fixing CO2 and adding oxygen); many (Porphyra, Laminaria, Sargassum) are eaten; agar (from Gelidium, Gracilaria) is used in lab cultures and foods.

examples.problem: Example 1: Name the three classes of algae with the main pigment of each.
examples.solution:
Algae are classified by pigment.

  • Chlorophyceae (green) — chlorophyll a and b.
  • Phaeophyceae (brown) — fucoxanthin.
  • Rhodophyceae (red) — r-phycoerythrin.

Algae are major producers.

  • They carry out about half of the total photosynthesis on Earth.
  • This fixes carbon dioxide and increases the oxygen in the environment.
examples.answer: Algae perform about half of all photosynthesis, fixing CO2 and adding oxygen to the environment.

examples.problem: Example 3: What is agar and from which algae is it obtained?
examples.solution:
Agar is a useful algal product.

  • It is a gel-like substance used to grow microbes in labs and in foods.
  • It is obtained from red algae such as Gelidium and Gracilaria.
examples.answer: Agar is a gelling substance (used in lab cultures and foods) obtained from red algae like Gelidium and Gracilaria.

recap:
• Plantae = multicellular, chlorophyll-bearing autotrophs: algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms, angiosperms.
  • Algae have a simple thallus; classes: Chlorophyceae (green, starch), Phaeophyceae (brown, fucoxanthin), Rhodophyceae (red, phycoerythrin).
  • Algae do ~half of Earth's photosynthesis; provide food and agar.

quiz.q: Brown algae (Phaeophyceae) get their colour from the pigment:
quiz.explanation: Fucoxanthin gives brown algae their brown colour.

quiz.q: The plant body of an alga, not differentiated into root, stem and leaf, is called a:
quiz.explanation: The simple, undifferentiated algal body is a thallus.

topics.title: Bryophytes and Pteridophytes
topics.concept:
Bryophytes are the 'amphibians of the plant kingdom' — they live on land but need water for sexual reproduction. The plant body is more differentiated than algae but lacks true roots, stem and leaves (it has root-like rhizoids). They have no vascular tissue (no xylem/phloem). The main plant body is the gametophyte (haploid). Examples include mosses (e.g. Funaria, Sphagnum) and liverworts (e.g. Marchantia). Bryophytes help in soil formation and prevent soil erosion; Sphagnum (peat moss) is used as fuel and packing material.

Pteridophytes are the first true land plants to have vascular tissue (xylem and phloem) and a body differentiated into true root, stem and leaves. They still need water for reproduction. Examples: ferns (Pteris, Adiantum), Selaginella, Equisetum (horsetail), Lycopodium. In pteridophytes the dominant plant body is the sporophyte (diploid), which bears spore-producing structures (sporangia) on leaf-like sporophylls; spores germinate into a small, free-living gametophyte (called the prothallus).

Most pteridophytes are homosporous (produce one kind of spore), but some (e.g. Selaginella, Salvinia) are heterosporous — they produce two kinds of spores (large megaspores and small microspores). This heterospory, where the female gametophyte is retained on the parent plant, is considered an important step towards the seed habit seen in higher plants.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why are bryophytes called the 'amphibians of the plant kingdom'?
examples.solution:
Bryophytes have a half-on-land, half-needing-water nature.

  • They live on land (in moist places).
  • But they need water for sexual reproduction (to allow the male gametes to swim to the female), just like amphibians.
examples.answer: Because they live on land but still need water for sexual reproduction, like amphibians.

examples.problem: Example 2: What major feature do pteridophytes have that bryophytes lack?
examples.solution:
Compare their internal tissue.

  • Pteridophytes have vascular tissue (xylem and phloem) and true roots, stems and leaves.
  • Bryophytes lack vascular tissue.
examples.answer: Pteridophytes have vascular tissue (xylem and phloem) and true roots, stems and leaves, which bryophytes lack.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why is heterospory in some pteridophytes significant?
examples.solution:
Heterospory is a step towards seeds.

  • Producing two kinds of spores, with the female gametophyte retained on the plant, foreshadows the seed habit.
examples.answer: Heterospory (two kinds of spores, with the female gametophyte retained on the parent) is an important precursor to the seed habit of higher plants.

recap:
• Bryophytes ('amphibians of plants'): land plants needing water to reproduce; no vascular tissue; dominant gametophyte (mosses, liverworts).
  • Pteridophytes: first plants with vascular tissue and true root/stem/leaves; dominant sporophyte; gametophyte = prothallus (ferns, Selaginella).
  • Most are homosporous; heterospory (in Selaginella, Salvinia) is a step towards the seed habit.

quiz.q: Which group is the first to have true vascular tissue (xylem and phloem)?
quiz.explanation: Pteridophytes are the first plants with vascular tissue.

quiz.q: In bryophytes, the dominant plant body is the:
quiz.explanation: The dominant phase in bryophytes is the haploid gametophyte.

topics.title: Gymnosperms, Angiosperms and Plant Life Cycles
topics.concept:
Gymnosperms (Greek gymnos = naked, sperma = seed) are plants that bear naked seeds — the seeds (ovules) are not enclosed inside a fruit. They are mostly evergreen, woody trees and shrubs. They have well-developed vascular tissue, but the xylem lacks vessels and the phloem lacks companion cells. Examples: Pinus, Cycas, Cedrus, Ginkgo. The dominant body is the sporophyte, bearing male and female cones; pollination is mostly by wind.

Angiosperms (angio = covered) are the flowering plants, in which seeds are enclosed inside a fruit (formed from the ovary). They are the most advanced and largest group of plants. They show double fertilisation (a unique feature) and have flowers as their reproductive organs. Angiosperms are of two classes: dicotyledons (two seed leaves, reticulate leaf venation, e.g. mango, pea) and monocotyledons (one seed leaf, parallel venation, e.g. wheat, grass).

In all plants, the life cycle shows an alternation of generations: a haploid (n) gametophyte phase alternates with a diploid (2n) sporophyte phase. There are three patterns:

  • Haplontic — the dominant phase is the haploid gametophyte; the diploid phase is just the zygote (e.g. many algae like Spirogyra).
  • Diplontic — the dominant phase is the diploid sporophyte; the gametophyte is greatly reduced (e.g. seed plants — gymnosperms and angiosperms).
  • Haplo-diplontic — both phases are multicellular and prominent (e.g. bryophytes and pteridophytes).

examples.problem: Example 1: What is the key difference between gymnosperms and angiosperms regarding seeds?
examples.solution:
The difference is whether the seed is covered.

  • Gymnosperms bear naked seeds (not enclosed in a fruit).
  • Angiosperms bear seeds enclosed inside a fruit.
examples.answer: Gymnosperms have naked (uncovered) seeds, while angiosperms have seeds enclosed within a fruit.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name and distinguish the two classes of angiosperms by their seed leaves and venation.
examples.solution:
Angiosperms are dicots and monocots.

  • Dicotyledons: two cotyledons, reticulate (net-like) leaf venation.
  • Monocotyledons: one cotyledon, parallel leaf venation.
examples.answer: Dicots (two seed leaves, reticulate venation) and monocots (one seed leaf, parallel venation).

examples.problem: Example 3: In seed plants (gymnosperms and angiosperms), which life-cycle pattern is shown?
examples.solution:
Seed plants are sporophyte-dominant.

  • The diploid sporophyte is dominant and the gametophyte is reduced.
  • This is the diplontic life cycle.
examples.answer: Seed plants show the diplontic life cycle (dominant diploid sporophyte, greatly reduced gametophyte).

recap:
• Gymnosperms = naked seeds (Pinus, Cycas); dominant sporophyte; wind pollination.
  • Angiosperms = flowering plants with seeds enclosed in a fruit; show double fertilisation; classes = dicots & monocots.
  • Alternation of generations: haploid gametophyte (n) alternates with diploid sporophyte (2n).
  • Patterns: haplontic (algae), diplontic (seed plants), haplo-diplontic (bryophytes, pteridophytes).

quiz.q: Plants that bear naked (uncovered) seeds are:
quiz.explanation: Gymnosperms bear naked seeds, not enclosed in a fruit.

quiz.q: Seed plants (gymnosperms and angiosperms) show which type of life cycle?
quiz.explanation: Seed plants are diplontic — the diploid sporophyte dominates.

questions.q: Members of Kingdom Plantae are mostly:
questions.explanation: Plants are eukaryotic, multicellular, chlorophyll-bearing autotrophs.

questions.q: The simple, undifferentiated plant body of an alga is a:
questions.explanation: Algae have a thallus, not differentiated into root, stem and leaf.

questions.q: Green algae (Chlorophyceae) store food mainly as:
questions.explanation: Green algae store food as starch and have cellulose walls.

questions.q: The brown colour of Phaeophyceae is due to:
questions.explanation: Fucoxanthin gives brown algae their colour.

questions.q: Agar, used in laboratory cultures, is obtained from:
questions.explanation: Agar comes from red algae such as Gelidium and Gracilaria.

questions.q: Bryophytes are called the 'amphibians of the plant kingdom' because they:
questions.explanation: They live on land but need water for reproduction, like amphibians.

questions.q: Bryophytes lack:
questions.explanation: Bryophytes have no vascular tissue.

questions.q: The first true land plants to have vascular tissue are the:
questions.explanation: Pteridophytes are the first plants with xylem and phloem.

questions.q: In pteridophytes, the dominant plant body is the:
questions.explanation: In pteridophytes the diploid sporophyte is dominant.

questions.q: Gymnosperms are characterised by:
questions.explanation: Gymnosperms bear naked seeds, not enclosed in a fruit.

questions.q: Angiosperms differ from gymnosperms because their seeds are:
questions.explanation: Angiosperm seeds are enclosed within the fruit.

questions.q: A unique feature of angiosperms is:
questions.explanation: Double fertilisation is unique to angiosperms.

questions.q: A plant with one cotyledon and parallel leaf venation is a:
questions.explanation: Monocots have one seed leaf and parallel venation.

questions.q: The alternation between a haploid gametophyte and a diploid sporophyte is called:
questions.explanation: Plants show alternation of generations between n and 2n phases.

questions.q: The life cycle of seed plants, with a dominant diploid sporophyte, is:
questions.explanation: Seed plants show the diplontic life cycle.

questions.q: Red algae can grow at greater ocean depths than green algae mainly because their pigment phycoerythrin:
options: Absorbs the blue-green light that penetrates deep water
questions.explanation: Phycoerythrin captures the blue-green light reaching deep water, letting red algae photosynthesise there.

questions.q: Heterospory in Selaginella is considered a precursor to the seed habit because:
options: The female gametophyte is retained and nourished on the parent sporophyte
It produces only one spore type
questions.explanation: Retention of the female gametophyte on the parent, as in heterospory, foreshadows the seed.

questions.q: Both bryophytes and pteridophytes still require water for reproduction because:
options: Their motile male gametes must swim to the female gamete
questions.explanation: In both groups the male gametes swim through water to reach the egg, so external water is needed.

questions.q: A diplontic life cycle is advantageous on land because the dominant diploid sporophyte:
options: Is better adapted, with vascular tissue, to survive land conditions
questions.explanation: The robust, vascularised diploid sporophyte copes better with terrestrial life than a delicate gametophyte.

questions.q: Why are gymnosperm seeds called 'naked'?
options: The ovules/seeds are not enclosed within an ovary or fruit
questions.explanation: Gymnosperm ovules sit exposed on cone scales, not enclosed in an ovary, so the seeds are 'naked'.

questions.q: A botanist finds a plant with flowers, fruits enclosing seeds, two cotyledons and net-like leaf venation. It is a:
questions.explanation: Flowers + fruit-enclosed seeds = angiosperm; two cotyledons + reticulate venation = dicot.
